title: The First Law of Thermodynamics and Some Simple Processes
lead: A heat engine is a machine that uses heat transfer to do work, and every heat engine is built from a few simple processes that follow from the first law. This section introduces the heat engine as a gas in a cylinder that takes in heat, pushes a piston and gives heat back; shows that the work done on or by a gas is the area under its path on a graph of pressure versus volume, and that the net work of a cycle is the area inside its loop; defines the isobaric, isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes and what the first law says about each; and explains why the reversible processes of theory are never quite achieved in practice.
objectives: Describe the processes of a simple heat engine.
Explain the differences among the simple thermodynamic processes—isobaric, isochoric, isothermal, and adiabatic.
Calculate total work done in a cyclical thermodynamic process.
summary_html:
• One of the important implications of the first law of thermodynamics is that machines can be harnessed to do work that humans previously did by hand or by external energy supplies such as running water or the heat of the Sun. A machine that uses heat transfer to do work is known as a heat engine.
  • There are several simple processes, used by heat engines, that flow from the first law of thermodynamics. Among them are the isobaric, isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes.
  • These processes differ from one another based on how they affect pressure, volume, temperature, and heat transfer.
  • If the work done is performed on the outside environment, work ($\kW$) will be a positive value. If the work done is done to the heat engine system, work ($\kW$) will be a negative value.
  • Some thermodynamic processes, including isothermal and adiabatic processes, are reversible in theory; that is, both the thermodynamic system and the environment can be returned to their initial states. However, because of loss of energy owing to the second law of thermodynamics, complete reversibility does not work in practice.

figures.original_caption: Schematic representation of a heat engine, governed, of course, by the first law of thermodynamics. It is impossible to devise a system where Q_out = 0, that is, in which no heat transfer occurs to the environment.

(a) Heat transfer to the gas in a cylinder increases the internal energy of the gas, creating higher pressure and temperature. (b) The force exerted on the movable cylinder does work as the gas expands. Gas pressure and temperature decrease when it expands, indicating that the gas’s internal energy has been decreased by doing work. (c) Heat transfer to the environment further reduces pressure in the gas so that the piston can be more easily returned to its starting position.
An isobaric expansion of a gas requires heat transfer to keep the pressure constant. Since pressure is constant, the work done is PΔV.

(a) A PV diagram in which pressure varies as well as volume. The work done for each interval is its average pressure times the change in volume, or the area under the curve over that interval. Thus the total area under the curve equals the total work done. (b) Work must be done on the system to follow the reverse path. This is interpreted as a negative area under the curve.

(a) The work done in going from A to C depends on path. The work is greater for the path ABC than for the path ADC, because the former is at higher pressure. In both cases, the work done is the area under the path. This area is greater for path ABC. (b) The total work done in the cyclical process ABCDA is the area inside the loop, since the negative area below CD subtracts out, leaving just the area inside the rectangle. (The values given for the pressures and the change in volume are intended for use in the example below.) (c) The area inside any closed loop is the work done in the cyclical process. If the loop is traversed in a clockwise direction, W is positive—it is work done on the outside environment. If the loop is traveled in a counter-clockwise direction, W is negative—it is work that is done to the system.

(a) The upper curve is an isothermal process (ΔT = 0), whereas the lower curve is an adiabatic process (Q = 0). Both start from the same point A, but the isothermal process does more work than the adiabatic because heat transfer into the gas takes place to keep its temperature constant. This keeps the pressure higher all along the isothermal path than along the adiabatic path, producing more work. The adiabatic path thus ends up with a lower pressure and temperature at point C, even though the final volume is the same as for the isothermal process. (b) The cycle ABCA produces a net work output.
The two cyclical processes shown on this PV diagram start with and return the system to the conditions at point A, but they follow different paths and produce different amounts of work.
A graph of pressure versus volume for the cyclical process ABCDA of a heat engine.

exercises.prompt: A great deal of effort, time, and money has been spent in the quest for the so-called perpetual-motion machine, which is defined as a hypothetical machine that operates or produces useful work indefinitely and/or a hypothetical machine that produces more work or energy than it consumes. Explain, in terms of heat engines and the first law of thermodynamics, why or why not such a machine is likely to be constructed.

answer.solution: Treat the machine as a heat engine and apply the first law to one cycle. Because the machine returns to the same state at the end of each cycle, its internal energy does not change, so $\kdEint = \kQh - \kW = 0$ and the work it puts out equals the net heat transfer into it, $\kW = \kQin - \kQout$. A machine that produces more work than the energy it consumes would have $\kW$ greater than $\kQin$, which the first law forbids: energy would be appearing from nowhere. A machine that runs indefinitely with no energy supplied would have $\kQin = 0$ and still put out work, which the same equation forbids as well. Even a machine that only tried to convert all of its heat input into work, with $\kQout = 0$, is never achieved in practice, since Figure 15.7 and the next sections show that some heat transfer to the environment always occurs. The first law alone rules out the first kind of perpetual-motion machine, and the second law, which the following sections state, rules out the rest.

exercises.prompt: One method of converting heat transfer into doing work is for heat transfer into a gas to take place, which expands, doing work on a piston, as shown in the figure below. (a) Is the heat transfer converted directly to work in an isobaric process, or does it go through another form first? Explain your answer. (b) What about in an isothermal process? (c) What about in an adiabatic process (where heat transfer occurred prior to the adiabatic process)?

answer.solution: Ask in each case what the first law, $\kdEint = \kQh - \kW$, says about the internal energy. (a) In an isobaric expansion the gas does work $\kW = \kPr\Delta V$, but its internal energy changes too: for an ideal gas at constant pressure the temperature rises as the volume grows, so $\kdEint$ is positive and the heat transfer in is greater than the work out. Part of the heat transfer goes into internal energy first, and only part becomes work. (b) In an isothermal process the temperature is constant, so for an ideal gas $\kdEint = 0$ and $\kQh = \kW$. Here the heat transfer is converted directly to work: just enough heat flows in to replace the work as it is done, and the internal energy of the gas is unchanged. (c) In an adiabatic process there is no heat transfer at all, $\kQh = 0$, so the work is done entirely at the expense of the internal energy, $\kdEint = -\kW$. The heat transfer that came earlier was stored as internal energy, and it is that stored energy, not a simultaneous heat transfer, that the gas now converts to work.

exercises.prompt: Would the previous question make any sense for an isochoric process? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: No. An isochoric process is one at constant volume, so the piston does not move, $\Delta V = 0$, and the gas does no work at all: on a $PV$ diagram the process is a vertical line that encloses no area. The first law then reads $\kdEint = \kQh$, which says that every joule of heat transfer into the gas goes into its internal energy and raises its pressure and temperature. There is no work for the heat transfer to be converted into, so the question of whether the conversion is direct does not arise.

exercises.prompt: We ordinarily say that $\kdEint = 0$ for an isothermal process. Does this assume no phase change takes place? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: Yes, it does. The statement rests on the internal energy of an ideal gas depending on its temperature alone, $\kEint = \tfrac{3}{2}Nk\kTemp$ for a monatomic gas, so that a constant temperature means a constant internal energy. During a phase change the temperature stays constant while heat transfer continues, as the latent heat of Chapter 14 describes, and that heat transfer goes into the internal energy of the substance, breaking or forming the bonds between its molecules. A liquid boiling at constant temperature therefore has $\kdEint$ greater than zero even though $\Delta T = 0$. The rule $\kdEint = 0$ for an isothermal process holds for an ideal gas with no phase change, which is what the passage assumes when it writes $PV = nR\kTemp$.

exercises.prompt: The temperature of a rapidly expanding gas decreases. Explain why in terms of the first law of thermodynamics. (Hint: Consider whether the gas does work and whether heat transfer occurs rapidly into the gas through conduction.)

answer.solution: An expanding gas pushes on its surroundings and so does work, $\kW$ positive. A rapid expansion leaves no time for heat transfer by conduction into the gas, so $\kQh$ is close to zero and the process is nearly adiabatic. The first law, $\kdEint = \kQh - \kW$, then gives $\kdEint = -\kW$: the work is done at the expense of the internal energy. For a gas the internal energy is the kinetic energy of its molecules, $\kEint = \tfrac{3}{2}Nk\kTemp$ for a monatomic gas, so a fall in internal energy is a fall in temperature. This is why a gas released from a pressurized cylinder comes out cold.

exercises.prompt: Which cyclical process represented by the two closed loops, ABCFA and ABDEA, on the $PV$ diagram in the figure below produces the greatest net work? Is that process also the one with the smallest work input required to return it to point A? Explain your responses.

answer.solution: The net work of a cyclical process is the area inside its loop on the $PV$ diagram. The loop ABDEA encloses the rectangle ABCF and the strip FCDE beneath it, so it has the larger area and produces the greater net work. The work input needed to return the system to A is the work done on the gas along the return legs, which is the area under the compression leg: for ABCFA that is the area under FC, and for ABDEA the area under ED. Since ED lies at a lower pressure than FC, the area under it is smaller, so ABDEA also needs the smaller work input on its way back to A. It does more work on the outward leg AB than it takes to return, and the difference, the enclosed area, is larger for the taller loop. The greatest net work and the smallest return work go to the same cycle here, because both loops share the expansion AB at the same pressure and differ only in how low the pressure drops for the compression.

exercises.prompt: A real process may be nearly adiabatic if it occurs over a very short time. How does the short time span help the process to be adiabatic?

answer.solution: An adiabatic process is one with no heat transfer, $\kQh = 0$. Heat transfer takes time: conduction moves energy at a rate set by the temperature difference, the material and the thickness it has to cross, and convection and radiation are no faster in a gas. If the process is over before any appreciable heat transfer has had time to occur, the total heat transfer during it is very small, and the process is close to adiabatic even without insulation. The faster the process, the less heat gets in or out, which is why the compression stroke of an engine and the sudden release of a compressed gas are treated as adiabatic.

exercises.prompt: It is unlikely that a process can be isothermal unless it is a very slow process. Explain why. Is the same true for isobaric and isochoric processes? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: An isothermal process keeps the temperature of the gas constant while it does work or has work done on it, and for an ideal gas that requires heat transfer equal to the work, $\kQh = \kW$, to flow in or out as the process goes on. Heat transfer takes time, and it must also spread through the gas so that no region is hotter or colder than the rest. If the process were fast, the work would be done before the heat could arrive and the temperature would change, as it does in an adiabatic process. So an isothermal process must be slow. The same is not required of an isobaric or an isochoric process. An isochoric process needs only that the volume be held fixed, which a rigid container does at any speed, and the temperature is then free to change. An isobaric process needs only that the pressure be held constant, which a freely moving piston under a fixed load does; the temperature changes along the way and no particular heat transfer has to keep pace with the work, so it too can be fast, provided the gas stays close to a uniform pressure.

exercises.prompt: Consider process CD in the figure below. Does this represent work done by or on the system, and how much?

answer.solution: Process CD runs from C, at a volume of $4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$, to D, at $1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$. The volume decreases, so $\Delta V$ is negative and the work is done on the system, not by it. Its size is the area under the line CD, a trapezoid $3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$ wide whose parallel sides are the pressures $0.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$ at C and $1.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$ at D. The average pressure along CD is therefore $0.8 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$, and $\kW = (0.8 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2)(-3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3) = -2.4 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}$. About $2.4 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}$ of work is done on the gas in process CD, and the minus sign records that it is work in rather than work out.

exercises.prompt: The first step of a thermodynamic cycle is an isobaric process with increasing volume. The second is an isochoric process, with decreasing pressure. The last step may be either an isothermal or adiabatic process, ending at the starting point of the isobaric process. Sketch a graph of these two possibilities, and comment on which will have greater net work per cycle.

answer.solution: Draw the axes with pressure upward and volume to the right and start at a point A. The isobaric step with increasing volume is a horizontal line from A to the right, to a point B. The isochoric step with decreasing pressure is a vertical line straight down from B to a point C. The last step must return from C to A, which lies up and to the left, so it is a compression along a curve that rises to the left. If it is isothermal the curve has $PV$ constant and is the gentler of the two; if it is adiabatic the pressure rises more steeply as the gas is compressed, because no heat leaves and the work done on the gas raises its temperature, so the adiabatic curve from C to A lies below the isothermal one for the same two endpoints. Both cycles are walked clockwise, so their net work is positive and equals the area inside each loop. The area enclosed is larger when the return curve lies lower, which is the adiabatic case, so the cycle closed by an adiabatic compression has the greater net work per cycle. Note that for the two curves to meet the same points C and A, the point C must be chosen differently in the two cases, since an isotherm and an adiabat through A pass through different points at the volume of B.

exercises.prompt: Look at the figure below, and assign values to the three pressures and two volumes given in the graph. Then calculate the net work for the cycle ABCFEDCFA using those values. How does this work compare to the heat output or input of the system? Which value(s) would you change to maximize the net work per cycle?

answer.solution: Choose values first, for example a pressure $P_1$ along AB, a lower pressure $P_2$ along FC, a still lower pressure $P_3$ along ED, and volumes $V_1$ at the left side AFE and $V_2$ at the right side BCD. Then follow the path leg by leg, taking the work as the area under each leg, positive where the volume increases and negative where it decreases, and zero along the vertical legs. The path ABCFEDCFA is two loops joined at F and C. The first, ABCF, is walked clockwise: the work along AB is $P_1(V_2 - V_1)$, along CF it is $-P_2(V_2 - V_1)$, and the net for that loop is $(P_1 - P_2)(V_2 - V_1)$, positive. The second, FEDC, is walked counterclockwise: down from F to E, right along ED at $P_3$ for $P_3(V_2 - V_1)$, up from D to C, and back left along CF for $-P_2(V_2 - V_1)$, a net of $-(P_2 - P_3)(V_2 - V_1)$, negative. The net work of the whole path is the sum, $(P_1 - P_2)(V_2 - V_1) - (P_2 - P_3)(V_2 - V_1)$, the area of the upper rectangle less the area of the lower strip. Because the system returns to A, its internal energy is unchanged and the first law gives $\kW = \kQin - \kQout$: the net work equals the net heat transfer into the system over the cycle. To make the net work per cycle as large as possible, raise $P_1$ or widen the volumes $V_2 - V_1$, which enlarge the clockwise loop, and bring $P_3$ up toward $P_2$, which shrinks the counterclockwise loop that takes work back in.

exercises.prompt: A car tire contains $0.0380\ \text{m}^3$ of nitrogen at a gauge pressure of $2.20 \times 10^{5}\ \text{N/m}^2$ (about 32 psi). How much more internal energy does this gas have than the same volume has at zero gauge pressure (which is equivalent to normal atmospheric pressure)? (Use $\kEint = \tfrac{5}{2}Nk\kTemp$ for the internal energy of nitrogen, a diatomic gas.)

answer.hint: The ideal gas law gives $Nk\kTemp = PV$, so the internal energy of the nitrogen is $\tfrac{5}{2}PV$ and the extra internal energy is $\tfrac{5}{2}\Delta P\,V$, with $\Delta P$ the gauge pressure.

exercises.prompt: Steam to drive an old-fashioned steam locomotive is supplied at a constant gauge pressure of $1.75 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}^2$ (about 250 psi) to a piston with a 0.200-m radius. (a) By calculating $\kPr\Delta V$, find the work done by the steam when the piston moves 0.800 m. Note that this is the net work output, since gauge pressure is used. (b) Now find the amount of work by calculating the force exerted times the distance traveled. Is the answer the same as in part (a)?

parts.hint: The process is isobaric, so $\kW = \kPr\Delta V$, and the change in volume is the area of the piston, $\pi r^2$, times the distance it moves.
The force on the piston is $\kF = \kPr A$ with $A = \pi r^2$, and the work is $\kF\kd$.

answer.solution: (a) $\kW = \kPr\Delta V = 1.76 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$ (b) $\kW = \kF\kd = 1.76 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$. Yes, the answer is the same.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results What is wrong with the claim that a cyclical heat engine does 4.00 kJ of work on an input of 24.0 kJ of heat transfer while 16.0 kJ of heat transfers to the environment?

answer.solution: $\kW$ is not equal to the difference between the heat input and the heat output.
